en: Heating liquid water adds energy, causing molecules to move faster and escape as water vapor gas.
Iron reacts with oxygen and water in the air to form a new, flaky brown substance called rust.
Stirring sugar into hot tea breaks the sugar crystals into tiny particles that spread evenly throughout the liquid.
Adding heat to solid butter gives its molecules enough energy to break their rigid structure and flow as a liquid.
Pumping air into a flat tire forces more gas molecules inside, increasing pressure to make the tire firm.
Baking powder releases carbon dioxide gas when heated, creating bubbles that make a cake batter rise and become fluffy.
Oil floats on water because oil molecules are packed less tightly, making oil less dense than water molecules.
Cooling warm water vapor removes energy, causing gas molecules to slow down and clump together into liquid dew drops.
Pouring muddy water through filter paper traps large solid dirt particles while allowing the liquid water to pass through.
Mixing vinegar and baking soda causes a chemical reaction that rapidly produces carbon dioxide gas, creating visible fizzing bubbles.
Leaving dry ice in a warm room gives its solid carbon dioxide molecules enough energy to turn directly into gas.
Shaking oil and vinegar temporarily mixes them, but they separate again because oil and water molecules repel each other.
